newsitem.title: JAPAN: Tokyo shares rocked again by concerns over economy.
newsitem.headline: Tokyo shares rocked again by concerns over economy.

text.p: Japanese shares tumbled Friday in a renewed sell-off that has sent the market down more than 15 percent in the past month and shows no signs of ending.
The key Nikkei average of 225 shares ended the morning session with a loss of 428.43 points at 17,645.44, a fall of 2.37 percent and below the key psychological level of 18,000.
Analysts said that there seems to be no end in sight, with bargain-hunting failing to emerge even as the market hits new lows.
"The market's slide doesn't appear to be stopping anytime soon," said Tadahiro Kamogawa, a senior analyst at Yamaichi Securities Co Ltd.

They say the market is being pushed down by concerns about the Japanese economy in the face of higher sales taxes from April, and a lack of government plans to help stimulate growth with any new spending programmes.
The fall, which gathered pace when trading began for the new year Monday, has continued despite attempts by government leaders to persuade the market that the economy is not all that bad.
Trade Minister Shinji Sato said after a cabinet meeting on Friday that the economy was set to recover in the latter half of the 1997/98 fiscal year, led by private demand.
He signalled that authorities would do no more than keep careful watch over the market at the moment.
"Japan must watch the stock market trend with caution," he said. But he added that the government has not discussed any measures to stem the fall.
Economic Planning Agency Minister Taro Aso, meanwhile, said that the market must be allowed to move freely. "It's not for the government to intervene," he told a news conference.
But analysts said that the government's policies are a key factor behind the stock market fall.

Faced with massive budget deficits, the government has gone ahead with a controversial plan to raise sales taxes beginning with the new fiscal year on April 1. In addition, it has been reluctant to institute a supplemental budget to help spur growth.
Financial markets are also concerned that the Japanese government may drag its feet in carrying out various administrative and financial reforms.

But Finance Minister Hiroshi Mitsuzuka reiterated the government's determination to carry out reform measures. "We are determined to carry out the reforms steadily and without fail," he told a news conference.

The decline in shares has been led by the banking industry, which is still trying to get out from under a virtual mountain of bad debts left over from the collapse of real estate values in the early 1990s.
Analysts note that the fall in share values is in turn putting more pressure on the banks since part of their earnings depend on profits from their own holdings in the stock market.
Analysts say there is no sign of a meltdown in Tokyo's financial markets.
The Japanese government bond market has taken the stock market fall calmly with virtually no impact on prices.
The yen was steady against the dollar after fears of possible dollar sales by Japanese authorities. The U.S. currency earlier this week hit its highest level in nearly four years.
